acceptedAnswer.text: Yes as a rehearsal of execution — no as a predictor of profit. It teaches order mechanics, sizing math, honest logging, and plan-following. It cannot teach drawdown psychology or execution friction. It is worth it if you know which questions it is allowed to answer — and whether you will make money is not one of them.

Two engines. First, execution fiction: paper fills at the quoted price, with no slippage, no bid-ask spread cost, no partial fills or rejections, and costs often ignored. Second, the psychological switch: fear, greed, ego, and expectations change the trader while the strategy stays identical. Same setups, different human. The first engine is mechanics; the second is the standard practitioner and behavioural explanation, not neuroscience.

mainEntity.name: Why do I make money paper trading but lose with real money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Competence, not a calendar. A common practitioner bar is: one plan, 20–50 logged trades with costs enabled, roughly 90% rule adherence (adherence = trades following every rule ÷ total trades), sizing at the intended live amounts — then the smallest real size. Those numbers are practitioner consensus with a wide published range (other protocols demand up to 100–200 trades or 3–6 months). They are never presented here as our research, a study, or a standard. Readiness is documented in your log, not felt.

mainEntity.name: How long should I paper trade before going live?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sitting through a real drawdown with money at stake, execution under real liquidity, and your own behavioural failure modes — moving stops, sizing up after wins, skipping signals. This is definitional: a zero-stakes simulation cannot, by construction, teach staked behaviour.

mainEntity.name: What does paper trading NOT teach you?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — as protocol advice, this is non-negotiable. An unrealistic paper balance rehearses decisions the live account will never face. The practical difference is minimum quantity and lot granularity, affordability of stops, and psychology — not a claim that percentages themselves change. Percentages are scale-free in pure arithmetic; the decisions, the fills, and the experience are not.

mainEntity.name: Should I paper trade with the same account size I plan to use live?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four rules: real account size; costs ON; log every fill as if it cost you; journal the rule breaks. Costs ON means real cost math at the verified 2026-10-14 rates in the Costs ON section above — STT, per-exchange charges, stamp duty, GST, SEBI charges, and your own broker's brokerage. The cost calculators are the correction for paper results that ignore this stack.

mainEntity.name: How do I make paper trading as realistic as possible?

acceptedAnswer.text: Small enough that a full losing streak at real size costs tuition, not trauma: the 1%-rule — a widely used risk-budgeting guideline, not a law — at the minimum viable size. At 1% risk per trade, five straight losses cost 4.90% of capital (1 − 0.99⁵ = 0.0490), under the same compounding assumption as the size-trap table. Small size buys time to learn. It does not create edge.

mainEntity.name: When I go live, how small should I start?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reconcile live performance against what the backtest predicted for the same period, over a minimum of 30 live trades and 4 weeks, on net P&L per trade after all costs. A gap of more than 25% below the backtest-predicted figure triggers a model review; a gap still present after two consecutive reviews is persistent — a modelling error (costs, fills, or regime), not bad luck. A short-term gap alone proves nothing; persistence is the signal. This is a discipline for staying honest, not an empirical finding — and the fix, when the gap persists, is in the model.
